title: How many, how much
goal: Count with native Tagalog numbers, read prices and times with Spanish numbers, and know which to use when.
bekal: count from 1 to 100 with the native Tagalog numbers
say prices with Spanish numbers — the way it's really done in the market
attach the linker to numbers: *isang libro*, *apat na bata*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Sa bakery
dialogs.intro: Morning at a bakery. Budi is buying pandesal, the small round rolls that are breakfast for millions of Filipinos.

lines.speaker: Tindera:
lines.text: Magandang umaga po! Ano po ang kailangan ninyo?
lines.id: Good morning, sir! What do you need?
lines.literal: beautiful-of morning sir! what sir si need your-all?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: How much is the pandesal, ma'am?

lines.speaker: Tindera:
lines.text: Sampung pandesal po. Trenta pesos lahat.
lines.id: Ten pandesal. Thirty pesos in all.
lines.literal: ten pandesal sir. thirty pesos all.

lines.speaker: Tindera:
lines.text: Bente pesos po ang sukli ninyo. Salamat po!
lines.id: Your change is twenty pesos, sir. Thank you!
lines.literal: twenty pesos ma'am si change your-all. thanks ma'am!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: May kape rin po ba kayo?
lines.id: Do you have coffee too, ma'am?

lines.speaker: Tindera:
lines.text: Mayroon po. Dalawampung piso ang isang tasa.
lines.id: Yes, sir. Twenty pesos a cup.
lines.literal: there-is ma'am. twenty peso si one cup.

lines.speaker: Tindera:
lines.text: Sige po. Balik po kayo, ha?
lines.id: Okay, sir. Come back again, okay?
lines.literal: all-right ma'am. return sir you-all, okay?

notes: **Two number systems live side by side.** The native Tagalog numbers (*isa, dalawa, tatlo*) are used to count things. The Spanish numbers (*uno, dos, tres*) are used for **prices, time and dates**. Neither replaces the other: the same person uses both in a single sentence, as in this dialogue.
**Magkano asks for price**, *ilan* asks for quantity. Don't mix them up: *Ilan ang pandesal?* asks how many rolls, *Magkano ang pandesal?* asks how many pesos.

**Numbers need a linker too.** *Sampung pandesal*, *tatlong piso*, *dalawampung piso* — all use *-ng* because the numbers end in a vowel. Those ending in a consonant use *na*: *apat na tao*, *anim na libro*, *siyam na araw*.
**Bawat isa** means "each one" or "per piece". Another form with the same meaning: *isahan*, and in conversation people often just say *tig-tatlo* (three each).
**Heto** means "here it is" — used when handing something over, like "here you go" in English. Its cousins: *hayan* (there it is, near you) and *hayun* (there it is, far away).
**Pesos or piso?** The Tagalog form is *piso*, the English/Spanish form is *pesos*. Both are used without strict rules, often in the same sentence. On written prices you'll see ₱ or "Php".
**Bigyan ninyo ako ng sampu** is polite and a little formal. At a stall, people more often just say the number: *Sampu po* — and that's enough.
**Ha? at the end of a sentence** softens a request or invitation, like "okay?" in English: *Balik po kayo, ha?* The tone is warm, not challenging.
**Pandesal** (from Spanish *pan de sal*, salt bread) is the national breakfast of the Philippines — and even though the name means "salt bread", it actually tastes slightly sweet.

grammars.title: Native Tagalog numbers
body: These numbers are used to count objects, people, days and ages. A few will feel familiar if you know Malay or Indonesian: *lima* (five) and *anim* (six, cf. *enam*) are from the same Austronesian roots.
after: The teens pattern: **labing-** + the units number, with sound adjustments (*labindalawa*, *labintatlo*, *labing-apat*). The tens pattern: number + **-mpu** or **-napu** (*dalawampu*, *tatlumpu*, *apatnapu*).
The connector **'t** (short for *at*, "and") goes between tens and units: *dalawampu't lima* (25), *limampu't anim* (56).
For age, native numbers are used: *Dalawampu't lima anong taon ako* — or more commonly, *Beinte singko anyos ako*, with Spanish numbers. You'll hear both.

grammars.title: Spanish numbers — for money and time
body: For prices and time, Filipinos almost always use Spanish numbers. Using native numbers here isn't wrong, but it sounds like reading from a textbook.
after: Prices are said straight followed by *pesos*: *bente pesos*, *singkwenta pesos*, *siyento singkwenta pesos* (150).
For big hundreds and thousands, people go back to a mixture: *isang libo* (1,000) is more usual than *mil*, but *dos mil* (2,000) is also often heard.
⚠️ Spanish numbers are **not** used to count objects. *Dos pandesal* sounds odd; the right form is *dalawang pandesal*.

blocks.text: Numbers and nouns are always joined with a linker, and its form follows the rule you know from unit 3: the last letter of the number decides.

Notice that only three of the first ten numbers use *na*: **apat**, **anim** and **siyam** — all ending in a consonant. The rest use the attached *-ng*. Memorize those three exceptions and the rest runs itself.
*Ilan* stands alone; when followed by a noun it becomes *ilang*: *Ilang tao?* (how many people), *Ilang piso?* (how many pesos). The same linker again.

blocks.title: Ordinals: pang-
items: *Una* stands alone because it comes from Spanish; the rest use the prefix **pang-** on the native numbers.

exercises.prompt: Write in words using native Tagalog numbers.
Fill in the right linker: na or -ng.
Convert these prices into the Spanish numbers normally used.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: tatlong araw — apat na tao — anim na buwan — siyam na taon — sampung piso — dalawampu't lima
Magkano po ang pandesal? — Tatlong piso bawat isa. — Trenta pesos lahat. — Ilan ba ang gusto mo? — Bente pesos ang sukli.
